tur47-0: If there is fever, feeling unwell, loss of appetite or weight loss along with the pain (without delay)
tur47-1: If there is marked swelling, redness or warmth around the heel and foot (without delay)
tur47-2: If the pain is constant or getting worse, or does not ease at night or at rest
tur47-3: If the pain is in one heel and gets rapidly worse over a few days despite reduced activity: Sever’s pain usually eases with rest, so other causes such as bone infection (osteomyelitis) need to be ruled out

tur47-6: It is a simple 9-point examination doctors use to assess joint mobility: bending the little finger back beyond 90 degrees, touching the thumb to the forearm, the elbow and the knee bending backwards more than 10 degrees (one point each for right and left), and placing the palms flat on the floor with the knees straight (one point). Under the 2017 international criteria, the threshold for generalised joint hypermobility is 6 in pre-pubertal children and adolescents, 5 in adults up to age 50 and 4 over age 50. It is not a self-diagnosis test; the diagnosis is made by a doctor. Note: the Ehlers-Danlos Society has announced that new diagnostic criteria for the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and hypermobility spectrum disorders will be published on 1 December 2026 and will replace the previous criteria; this page will be updated to the new criteria.
